questions.q: Ada was charged ₦14,000 but "My orders" showed ₦12,500. What is the real cause?
questions.explain: Every read that re-derives a business decision is a second copy of the rules, and copies drift. A read model built from what the write side decided (the total in the event) cannot disagree with it.
options: The page query used sum on integers and lost precision
The page recomputed the total from the lines and did not know the delivery-fee rule that the write side applied
The order was placed in a transaction that had not committed yet
The read model was eventually consistent and had not caught up

questions.q: A new rule says a customer may have at most 5 open orders. Where must it be enforced?
questions.explain: The read model may be seconds behind, so any check against it can let a sixth order through. Rules are enforced where the truth is: the write model, in the transaction that makes the change.
options: In the projector that maintains order_summaries
In the ListMyOrders query, by counting rows
In the PlaceOrder command handler, against the write model, inside its transaction
In the API layer, by reading the read model before sending the command

questions.q: Who writes to order_summaries in the lesson's design?
questions.explain: One writer per read model keeps it consistent with the events and makes it rebuildable. If command handlers also wrote to it, a rebuild from events would not reproduce what they wrote.
options: The command handlers, right after they change orders
Only the projector, from recorded events
The query handlers, when a row is missing
The relay, when it publishes a row

questions.q: Right after a successful POST /orders, GET /orders/ORD-1042?minVersion=1 answers 503 with Retry-After: 1. Why is that better than a 404?
questions.explain: Eventual consistency has to be visible in the API. The client passed the version it just received, the server could see it was behind, and it said so with a status that means "temporarily unavailable, retry".
options: A 404 cannot carry a JSON body
503 responses are cached by browsers, 404 responses are not
The order exists; the read model has not caught up. 404 would make the app tell Ada her new order was not found, while 503 with Retry-After says "try again shortly"
A 404 would roll back the command

questions.q: What does expectedVersion on CancelOrder protect against?
questions.explain: This is optimistic concurrency. The UPDATE … WHERE version = $expected matches only if nothing changed since the client read the order. Ownership is a separate check (customer_id).
options: Two orders getting the same id
Events being applied twice by the projector
Acting on a stale page: a change made from an old view of the order is refused with a conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer change
Customers cancelling each other's orders

questions.q: Tunde tries to cancel Ada's order ORD-1. Why does the command answer NotFoundError rather than a "forbidden" error?
questions.explain: Answering the same way for "does not exist" and "not yours" avoids leaking which ids exist. The query side does the same by filtering on the signed-in customer.
options: Because the order really does not exist in the read model
Because "forbidden" would confirm to Tunde that ORD-1 exists; "not found" tells an outsider nothing
Because @zudojs/errors has no forbidden error
Because the version did not match

questions.q: Why does the client choose the order id in PlaceOrder?
questions.explain: A timeout does not tell the client whether the order was placed. With a client-generated id (a UUID in a real app), sending the same command again is safe: the handler finds the existing order and returns its result.
options: So the database needs no primary key
So a retried request with the same id can be recognised and answered with the first result instead of placing a second order
So the projector can sort orders alphabetically
Because @zudojs/cqrs requires every command to carry an id

questions.q: Why does PlaceOrder read the product with SELECT … FOR UPDATE before decrementing the stock?
questions.explain: Without the lock, two transactions can both read stock 1, both pass the check and both decrement. The CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint is a last line of defence, but the lock makes the check itself correct.
options: Because PGlite cannot run UPDATE without it
It locks the row, so a second checkout for the same product waits and then sees the new stock, instead of both seeing "1 left" and both selling it
It makes the query read-only
It publishes an event when the stock changes

questions.q: Tunde's order reserved 1 bottle of oil, then failed on the rice. Afterwards the oil stock is unchanged. Why?
questions.explain: manager.run commits when the callback returns and rolls back when it throws. Every change the command made, including the outbox row it never reached, disappears together.
options: The projector restored the oil when it saw the failure
The command handler caught the error and added the oil back
Both reservations ran in one transaction, and the thrown ConflictError made manager.run roll the whole transaction back
The oil was never reserved, because rice is checked first

questions.q: With plain @zudojs/cqrs, what does await bus.execute<PlaceOrder, { receiptUrl: string }>(command) do when the handler returns { orderId, version, totalKobo }?
questions.explain: The result type argument is not connected to the handler, so it is a claim. The typed facade in the lesson derives the result type from one map for both registration and execution, which turns this mistake into a compile error.
options: It fails to compile, because the handler returns a different type
It throws at runtime, because the result does not match
It compiles, and at runtime the result is the handler's object, so result.receiptUrl is undefined
It converts the result to the requested type

questions.q: The typed facade contains one cast, bus.execute(request, context) as Promise<never>. Why is that acceptable?
questions.explain: You cannot avoid the claim entirely, because the bus stores handlers in an untyped table. You can make it once, in a place whose other half (registration) enforces the same types.
options: Casts are free at runtime, so they are always acceptable
It is the only claim in the codebase, and it is guaranteed by construction: register only accepts handlers whose return type matches the same map entry
Because never disables type checking for the caller
Because the underlying bus validates results at runtime

questions.q: What does putting @CommandHandlerFor("CancelOrder") on a class do?
questions.explain: The decorator marks; it does not wire. bus.has("CancelOrder") stays false until something reads getCommandHandlerMetadata and registers an instance. Forgetting that step only shows up at runtime.
options: It registers a new instance of the class on every command bus
It registers the class on the default command bus
It only attaches metadata to the class; startup code must read it and call bus.register
It makes the class's execute method run in a transaction

questions.q: The read model of ORD-7 is at version 1, and the projector receives the event with version 3. What does it do, and why?
questions.explain: Only the next version is applied. A gap means an earlier event is still on its way (for example a retry), and the queue's retry gives it time to arrive.
options: Applies it, because newer is better
Skips it as a duplicate
Throws, so the queue retries it later: version 2 is missing, and applying 3 first could produce a state that never existed
Rebuilds the whole read model

questions.q: The event-driven lesson used a processed_events table for idempotency. Why does this projector not need one?
questions.explain: When events of one aggregate are numbered, the version does the job of the processed-events table and also detects out-of-order delivery. Without versions, you need the table.
options: Because the queue never delivers a job twice
Because the read row stores the last applied version, and every event carries its version, so "already applied" is simply event.version <= row.version
Because query handlers remove duplicates when they read
Because PostgreSQL ignores duplicate inserts automatically

questions.q: Why do the query handlers run in readOnly transactions?
questions.explain: "A query never changes anything" becomes a rule the database enforces, not a convention. The lesson's example tried a DELETE in a read-only transaction and got "cannot execute DELETE in a read-only transaction".
options: Read-only transactions skip the adapter's lock
PostgreSQL then refuses any write, so a query handler cannot change data even by mistake
Because the read model table is marked read-only
So that queries see uncommitted changes from commands

questions.q: Why does the command store the traceparent in the outbox row instead of relying on AsyncLocalStorage?
questions.explain: Every storage boundary (a table, a queue, a broker message) breaks the chain. Context crosses it only if you write it down on one side and restore it on the other.
options: AsyncLocalStorage only works in the browser
AsyncLocalStorage follows one chain of calls; the relay runs later, in its own chain, so the trace has to travel inside the data it reads
The outbox needs a unique column
To make the event id unique

questions.q: What does a QueueContextCarrier passed to createInMemoryQueue({ contextCarriers }) do?
questions.explain: The lesson's carrier captured the current traceparent and restored it by starting a consumer span with that parent, so the projection joined the request's trace.
options: It copies the whole AsyncLocalStorage store into the job
Its capture() runs at add() and stores a small value with the job; its restore() wraps the processor so the job runs inside that context
It retries jobs whose context is missing
It encrypts the job's payload

questions.q: The queue discards any value a caller puts in job metadata under its own key "zudo:context". Why?
questions.explain: Context that decides behaviour (a tenant, for example) must come from the trusted side. Letting any enqueuer set it would let one tenant's request run work as another.
options: To save memory
So code that adds jobs cannot forge the tenant, correlation id or trace a job runs under; only the queue's carriers write that key
Because metadata must be JSON
Because the key is reserved for dead letters

questions.q: What makes it possible to delete order_summaries and rebuild it?
questions.explain: Replaying the recorded events through the projector reproduces the read model. That only holds if nothing else writes to it and the events are kept.
options: PGlite keeps a backup of every table
Every change is also recorded as an event with its version in the outbox, and the projector is the read model's only writer
The query handlers cache every row
The write model has the same columns as the read model

questions.q: While backfilling customer_stats, the projector had to remember each order's total from order.placed to handle order.cancelled. What does that teach?
questions.explain: Design events with their consumers in mind: the facts that happened, with enough context to use them. Not everything, but not so little that every projector needs its own memory.
options: Cancellation events should never be recorded
Read models must be built from the write tables instead
Events must carry enough information for the read models you will build later, or projectors have to keep extra state
Totals should be recomputed in every projector
Events should always contain the whole database row

questions.q: Where is full CQRS (separate read models fed by events) most likely not worth it?
questions.explain: A small form over one table gains nothing from a projector, a queue and eventual consistency. Use a transaction and a query over the same table, and keep CQRS for reads that really differ from the writes.
options: A busy order history list read far more often than orders are placed
A support dashboard that combines data from several parts of the system
An admin form that edits a shop's opening hours
A search page served from a search index

questions.q: A projector applies an event only when its version is the next one. What does this print?
questions.explain: Version 2 is refused before 1 arrives, the repeated 1 is a duplicate, 3 is refused while 2 is missing, and then 2 and 3 apply in order. The final state is the same as if every event had arrived once, in order.
options: 2:gap at v2 1:applied 1:duplicate 3:gap at v3 2:applied 3:applied
2:applied 1:duplicate 1:duplicate 3:applied 2:duplicate 3:duplicate
2:gap at v2 1:applied 1:applied 3:gap at v3 2:applied 3:applied
2:gap at v2 1:applied 1:duplicate 3:applied 2:duplicate 3:duplicate

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second type argument of execute is a claim. At runtime the caller gets whatever the handler returned, which has no total.
options: undefined orderId,version
0 orderId,version
undefined total
TypeError: result.total is not defined

questions.q: Two browser tabs cancel the same order, both having loaded version 1. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second tab's version is stale, so it is refused with the current version. A request with the current version still fails, because a cancelled order cannot be cancelled again. Checking the version first tells a stale client to reload.
options: 200 v2 | 409 now at v2 | 409 already cancelled | 404
200 v2 | 200 v3 | 409 already cancelled | 404
200 v2 | 409 already cancelled | 409 now at v2 | 404

questions.q: A command causes another command. What does this print?
questions.explain: A child context keeps who is asking and the correlation id, gets its own request id, and records the parent's request id as its causationId. Contexts are frozen, like commands and events.
options:
cus_ada req-7f3a http
true false true

undefined req-7f3a http
true false true

cus_ada undefined http
false false true

cus_ada req-7f3a http
true true false

questions.q: The client retries PlaceOrder after a timeout. What does this print?
questions.explain: The retry finds the order with the same id and returns it, so stock is reserved once. Another customer reusing the id is a conflict, not a silent overwrite.
options: true 1 1 order id ORD-1 is taken
false -1 2 undefined
true 1 1 undefined
false 1 1 order id ORD-1 is taken

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The version check comes first: a client that says it produced version 1 of ORD-2 knows the order exists, so a missing row means "not projected yet", not "not found". Without minVersion, a missing row is a plain 404.
options: 200 placed v1 | 503 retry-after 1 | 503 retry-after 1 | 404
200 placed v1 | 200 placed v1 | 404 | 404
200 placed v1 | 503 retry-after 1 | 404 | 404
200 placed v1 | 404 | 503 retry-after 1 | 404

questions.q: A read model is rebuilt by folding the recorded events in order. What does this print?
questions.explain: Replaying the events gives the current state: ORD-2 ends cancelled at version 2, and the two open orders total ₦100,000. The cancelled order keeps its total in its row; it is just not counted as open.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The timing middleware sees every request, failed ones included, before the error reaches the caller. It also receives the execution context, which is how the lesson's log lines carry the correlation id.
options:
PlaceOrder ok 4bf92f35
CancelOrder failed 4bf92f35
caller saw the error
timed: 2

PlaceOrder ok 4bf92f35
caller saw the error
timed: 1

PlaceOrder ok undefined
CancelOrder failed undefined
caller saw the error
timed: 2

questions.q: Two cancels for the same order run at the same time, with and without lockMiddleware. What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a lock, both handlers read before either writes: the classic lost-update shape. lockMiddleware takes a lock per key (here per order) before the handler runs, so the second command starts only after the first finished. Optimistic concurrency detects this race; a lock prevents it, at the cost of waiting.
options:
unlocked: A reads, B reads, A writes, B writes
locked:   A reads, A writes, B reads, B writes

unlocked: A reads, A writes, B reads, B writes
locked:   A reads, A writes, B reads, B writes

unlocked: A reads, B reads, A writes, B writes
locked:   A reads, B reads, A writes, B writes

unlocked: A reads, B reads, B writes, A writes
locked:   B reads, B writes, A reads, A writes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ORD-1 v2 and ORD-2 v1 are not applied yet. Projection lag is the number to chart and alert on: a read model far behind looks like a bug to customers.

questions.q: Two modules register a handler for the same command. What does this print?
questions.explain: A command has exactly one handler, and the bus enforces it when the second registers, usually at startup. The first handler stays in place.
options:
true A command handler is already registered for "PlaceOrder".
orders module
legacy checkout

true A command handler is already registered for "PlaceOrder".

questions.q: Write project(row, event) for an order-summary read model. row is the current summary or undefined. Return { row, outcome }: if event.version is not above the row's version (0 when there is no row), return the row unchanged with outcome "duplicate"; if it is not exactly one more, throw an Error with the message gap; otherwise apply it (order.placed creates { status: "placed", totalKobo, version }, order.cancelled sets status "cancelled" and the new version) with outcome "applied".
questions.explain: Compare with the current version first; that single rule handles duplicates and ordering. The cancelled row keeps the total it had, because order.cancelled does not carry one.

questions.q: Finish cancelOrder(orders, customerId, orderId, expectedVersion). Throw Error("not found") when the order is missing or belongs to another customer; throw Error("stale: now vN") when the version differs; throw Error("already STATUS") when the status is not "placed"; otherwise set status "cancelled", increase the version and return the new version.
questions.explain: Ownership first (and answered like "missing", so ids do not leak), then the version, then the business rule. The order of checks decides which message the client gets, so it is part of the design.
questions.expected:
ORD-1 -> not found
ORD-1 -> 2
ORD-1 -> stale: now v2
ORD-2 -> already shipped
ORD-9 -> not found

questions.q: Write customerStats(events) that backfills a new read model from recorded events, in order. order.placed has orderId, customerId and totalKobo; order.cancelled has only orderId. Return an object mapping each customer to { orders, spentKobo }, where a cancelled order no longer counts.
questions.explain: The cancellation event does not say whose order it was or what it cost, so the projector keeps the placed orders it has seen. That extra memory is the price of a thin event.

questions.q: Write a @zudojs/cqrs middleware audit that pushes "TYPE by USER corr=CORRELATION" into lines before calling the handler, using "anonymous" when the context has no user. It must pass the request and context on and return the handler's result.
questions.explain: Always return next(request, context): forgetting the return makes every command return undefined, and not calling next skips the handler. The context is how the correlation id reaches code that has no access to the HTTP request.

questions.q: Finish placeOrder(state, customerId, orderId, lines) over an in-memory write model. It is idempotent by orderId (same customer: return the stored result; other customer: throw Error("taken")). It checks every line first and throws Error("only N of SKU left") without changing any stock if one fails. Otherwise it reserves the stock, stores and returns { orderId, totalKobo }, and pushes an event { type: "order.placed", orderId, version: 1 } to state.outbox.
questions.explain: Checking every line before changing anything is what a transaction gives you for free in the database: no half-reserved order. The retry returns the stored result and records no second event.

questions.q: Write toStatus(error) for the API layer: ValidationError → 400, AuthenticationError → 401, NotFoundError → 404, ConflictError → 409, ServiceUnavailableError → 503, and anything else → 500. Decide by error.name.
questions.explain: Every error a client can cause maps to a precise 4xx, so the client knows what to do next; anything unexpected is a 500. The @zudojs/errors classes carry these statuses as statusCode already, which is what the router uses; this table makes the decision explicit.

questions.q: Write the client side of read-your-writes: async function readAfterWrite(get, minVersion, maxTries) calls get(minVersion), which returns { status, body }. While the status is 503 and tries remain, it waits 10 ms and tries again. It returns { tries, status } of the last response.
questions.explain: Here the fake read model catches up on the fourth request. The first read succeeds then; the second gives up after three tries because version 2 never arrives, and the app can show "still processing" instead of waiting forever. A real client would also honour the Retry-After header.
